reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact metrics as a hitter and the xERA as a pitcher both sit at the same elite tier, which is the whole absurdity of this profile. At the plate, a 16.7% barrel rate and 15.0% walk rate coexist with a 28.7% whiff rate that looks like a liability until you realize the power and patience more than compensate — a projected .945 OPS across 691 plate appearances is what that balance produces. On the mound, a 2.70 xERA backed by 98.1 mph and 2486 rpm of fastball spin explains why hitters are squaring him up at just 87.4 mph average exit velocity, which is the real story of his pitching profile. The one dependency is availability: everything here assumes he holds together as a two-way player for a full Dodger season, and if the workload forces a choice, you're still looking at a franchise-caliber performer on whichever side survives.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-seven projected home runs at 22 years old, and the Statcast profile already backs the number up. At 93.2 mph average exit velocity and a 51.6% hard-hit rate, Caminero hits the ball about as hard as anyone in the sport, and a 12.4% walk rate, well above what you expect from someone swinging this aggressively, means pitchers can't simply nibble their way around him. The chase and whiff rates are middling, so the strikeouts are manageable rather than a warning sign. Third base defense is the dependency: the OAA profile is about as bad as it gets, and if he has to move off the position, the offensive ceiling carries him to a corner outfield or DH regular rather than a franchise cornerstone, but either way the bat plays.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power tension pulls this profile in two directions at once: a 22.8% barrel rate and 95.1 mph average exit velocity both at the 100th percentile, sitting next to a 28.5% strikeout rate that ranks near the bottom of the league. He doesn't chase at 22.2%, so the swing-and-miss lives inside the zone, which means pitchers can attack him and still lose badly when he connects. A .434 xwOBA and .620 xSLG say the damage is severe enough to carry the strikeouts, and a 17.3% walk rate keeps the plate appearances flowing. If the barrel rate holds at scale, the projected .268/.391/.531 line with 40 home runs becomes a conversation about MVP ballots; if pitchers learn to beat him inside the zone consistently, you're left with a .391 OBP and walks carrying a lineup spot.

The chase rate, 36.0%, is the thing to watch: he's expanding the zone more than most hitters with his production markers, which means pitchers have a clear path to exploit him if he doesn't tighten it up. If the discipline holds roughly where it is, the projection looks like a 33-homer, 37-steal outfielder hitting .277 with an .864 OPS in 686 plate appearances, the kind of five-category contributor who earns a lineup spot on merit alone. If pitchers start winning the chase-rate battle consistently, you're left with real speed, real contact quality, and a strikeout problem that limits the ceiling.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the one jagged edge in an otherwise elite profile. Kurtz's 58.3% hard-hit rate and 18.4% walk rate are both genuinely rare, and the .379 xwOBA reflects a hitter who does serious damage when he connects. The problem is a 36.8% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league, and whether those two things can coexist at scale is the whole argument. The projection says they can, landing at .263/.394/.505 with 36 projected home runs, essentially betting that the walk rate and raw power are loud enough to carry the strikeouts — and the xSLG of .493 suggests the batted-ball shape backs that up. If the whiff rate doesn't soften as he sees more big-league looks, the average erodes and the profile slides from star to streaky slugger; if it does, you have a middle-of-the-order first baseman with an uncommon combination of patience and thump.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the ERA projection comes in at 3.32, and the gap between those two numbers is where the whole argument lives. Skenes misses bats at a 29.3% clip while walking just 5.5%, a combination that makes the contact management almost secondary — the xwOBA against is .259, and hitters simply aren't squaring him up with enough frequency to matter. The whiff rate (27.8%) and chase rate (33.5%) are good rather than elite, which means the strikeout volume is built on the walk suppression as much as pure swing-and-miss; if the command slips, the strikeout total softens before anything else does. At 23 and projecting for 181.7 innings at a 1.06 WHIP, he's already a mid-rotation anchor at his floor and a genuine ace if the peripherals hold.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: A .471 xwOBA with a 100th-percentile finish tells you almost everything, but the shape underneath it is what makes the number feel conservative. His 18.8% barrel rate and 94.7 mph average exit velocity sit at the outer edge of what the Statcast era has measured, and a 14.4% walk rate means pitchers don't get to pick their spots against him. The projection of 46 home runs and a 1.012 OPS across 676 plate appearances is built on contact quality that has held across multiple full seasons, so the question isn't whether the bat plays — it's whether his body stays available, because at 24.7 ft/s he's not buying back anything with his legs if he misses time. Full health, he's one of the two or three most dangerous hitters in the American League; limited availability is the only version of this profile that comes up short.

That speed reading makes the baserunning projection almost impossible to take at face value, and if the stolen base total regresses hard, the offensive profile underneath is thin: .706 OPS projected, an 87.5 mph average exit velocity in the bottom quarter of the league, a 4.7% barrel rate. What he genuinely does well is make contact, a 12.4% strikeout rate in the 92nd percentile, with a whiff rate that backs it up, so the .319 xwOBA staying around average is believable enough. The whole case for a useful regular hinges on what that stolen base number actually looks like over a full season, because without it you're left with a low-OBP, below-average-power first baseman who doesn't carry the position on the bat alone.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The 14.9% walk rate, 96th percentile, is doing more work in this profile than the barrel numbers, and that's the point. Reynolds doesn't need to punish every mistake because he barely chases anything: a 23.1% chase rate in the 86th percentile keeps the count in his favor, which is where his .368 xwOBA gets built. The whiff rate at 28.9% is the friction in the profile, a real drag against contact quality that explains why the xBA sits at .259 despite hard contact on nearly half his batted balls. If the strikeouts creep up without the walk rate holding, the floor is a productive second-division regular; if the discipline holds, that projected .829 OPS understates what he is, a patient hard-hitting corner bat who earns his counting stats through plate control more than raw thunder.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a riddle: an 18.9% whiff rate sitting well above league average, paired with a 39.9% chase rate that lands near the bottom of the league. He makes contact when he swings, but he's swinging at a lot of bad pitches. That tension is why the projected .312 OBP feels like a ceiling, not a floor, and why 697 projected plate appearances of .265/.312/.399 puts him squarely in second-division regular territory rather than anywhere near an impact bat. The xBA at .285 says the hit tool is genuine and will carry him; the 5.8% walk rate says the rest of the offensive profile is built on sand if the contact ever softens.

reports.name: Kyson Witherspoon
reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 65.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The 5.10 ERA is loud, but the translation is the actual problem. Across 65.7 innings at A+, Witherspoon's stuff maps to a 7.7 K/9 against a major-league average closer to 8.6, and the walk rate translates to 4.4 at the big-league level against a context where 3.2 is ordinary, leaving a K-BB% equivalent of 10.5% when the average sits at 13.5%. The shape grades out below average across the board: a 45 on miss, 40s on command and dominance, and a floor that's relief depth if the control doesn't sharpen. The ceiling here, two to three years out, is a back-end starter, and only if the walk rate closes on the gap, because there isn't a second carrying tool to bail him out if it doesn't.

reports.name: JJ Wetherholt
reports.published_report: The chase rate tells the story before anything else: 22.4% puts him in the top tier of contact discipline, and the strikeout rate backs it up at 15.3%. The projection fills out to .265/.359/.412 with 22 home runs and 15 steals across 694 plate appearances, which is a quietly valuable second baseman, not a star, but a player who contributes across enough categories to matter. The ceiling here depends on whether the exit velocity stays useful in a major-league environment; the profile works because he controls the zone and puts the ball in play hard, and if the contact quality slips, you're left with a smart but limited regular.

reports.name: Riley Greene
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power side of this profile is convincing: a 14.0% barrel rate, 50.0% hard-hit rate, and 91.6 mph average exit velocity all cluster in the same upper tier, and an .485 xSLG says the 24 projected home runs aren't borrowed from luck. The walk rate at 12.8% is genuine, a real source of the .366 OBP, and a 24.3% chase rate shows the discipline isn't passive. The whole thing hinges on the strikeout rate — a 29.8% whiff rate and 26.5% K% drag against everything else, and if pitchers sharpen their attack inside the zone, the batting average projection softens before anything else does. What you get if the swing-and-miss stays manageable is a mid-lineup outfielder posting .831 OPS across 670 plate appearances; what you get if it doesn't is a streaky three-true-outcomes type who underperforms the raw contact quality every season.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 3.8% strikeout rate is not a typo. Arraez makes contact at a level that breaks the usual tradeoffs — the whiff rate sits at the 100th percentile while exit velocity (87.1 mph) and barrel rate (0.6%) sit near the bottom of the league, which is the whole tension in this profile: he hits everything and hits almost none of it hard. The xBA of .289 reflects that the contact is placed well enough to fall in; the .309 xwOBA reflects that soft contact, however well-aimed, caps what he can do with runners on base and limits the ceiling to a .797 OPS even across a full 683 PA. If his ability to spray the ball into gaps holds up on the move to San Francisco, he's a .319-hitting everyday player who gives you almost nothing to worry about in the strikeout column and almost nothing to dream about in the power column.

reports.name: Randy Arozarena
reports.published_report: The case for Arozarena in Seattle is quieter than his reputation, and that's actually the point. His 91.4 mph average exit velocity and .353 xwOBA hold up as a profile of a guy who makes consistent, quality contact without needing elite barrel rates to do damage, and the projection of .266/.362/.434 with 19 home runs and 29 steals across 646 plate appearances reflects exactly that shape. The sprint speed at 26.9 ft/s is ordinary, so those steals come from reads and instincts, not raw burst, which means the stolen-base number is the piece most sensitive to age. If the legs quietly lose another step, you're left with a solid everyday outfielder whose value lives entirely in on-base percentage and gap power, which is a fine thing to be.

His 90.7 mph average exit velocity grades well, but a 31.3% whiff rate drags his xBA down to .208, and the contact quality can't overcome the contact frequency: xwOBA sits at .292, well below a league-average hitter. The dependency is simple: the chase rate stays a liability, and the gap between what he hits and what he produces stays wide.

reports.name: Braxton Ashcraft
reports.published_report: The 37.3% chase rate is the engine here — that's elite territory, and it explains why the walk rate sits at a tidy 5.7% even though the 27.4% whiff rate is only ordinary. Ashcraft gets outs the quiet way: a 3.17 xERA and .278 xwOBA without generating a ton of swing-and-miss inside the zone, just a 97.2 mph fastball that backs hitters off the plate and forces bad decisions on pitches away. The contact allowed when hitters do connect is soft enough, 90.2 mph average exit velo, that the barrel rate holds at 6.0%, and the whole profile adds up to a mid-rotation starter rather than a strikeout artist pretending to be one. Everything here hinges on that chase rate holding; if opposing hitters stop chasing and start sitting on the fastball, his whiff numbers don't have the slack to cover it.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 56 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 12.1 K/9 at AA, translating to 9.3 against major-league hitters, which sits above a league average of 8.6, but the walks are eating the profile alive. Thirty-three free passes in 56 innings, translating to 4.6 walks per nine in an MLB context where the baseline is 3.2, leaves a K-BB% that barely reaches league average once you run it through the converter. The skill shape here is a 70-grade miss sitting on top of 30-grade command, and that combination either forces a relief conversion or demands a significant mechanical correction before the ETA window of one to two years closes. If the walks come down, there's a back-end starter; if they don't, what's left is a depth arm who strikes guys out and nothing else.

reports.name: Byron Buxton
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells you what he is: 18.7% puts him in the 98th percentile, and when he makes contact, the ball travels. An .xSLG of .517 backs that up, and the projection's .546 SLG with 37 home runs over 552 plate appearances is just that profile running hot and healthy. The problem isn't the bat, it's the two numbers sitting at the 18th and 23rd percentiles — a 30.9% whiff rate and 34.7% chase rate that keep the xBA at .250 and the walk rate at 6.9%, which is why a hitter this dangerous projects to a .324 OBP. If he stays upright for a full season, you're looking at a middle-of-the-order force; if the availability record reasserts itself, you're left with a part-time slugger who can't do enough damage in limited time to carry a roster spot.

reports.name: Brice Turang
reports.published_report:
The contact and chase numbers are pulling in opposite directions, and that tension defines the Turang read. He walks at 12.7% and chases just 24.0% of the time, a genuinely elite feel for the zone. But a 25.4% strikeout rate undercuts what that discipline should produce, meaning pitchers are beating him inside the zone more than the chase number alone would suggest.

The Statcast profile backstops the projection anyway: 90.9 mph average exit velocity and a .346 xwOBA say the contact quality holds up even when the contact rate is shaky. Add 28.6 ft/s sprint speed and the projection's 26 stolen bases become easy to picture. If the strikeout rate drifts toward something more in line with his 21.8% whiff rate, you get a .262/.350/.435 second baseman with 20 home runs and a 95th-percentile glove, a legitimate everyday contributor rather than just a good-tools guy.

reports.name: Iván Herrera
reports.published_report: The whole argument lives in the gap between his .351 xwOBA and his .390 xSLG: elite contact quality by one measure, middling slug by another, and the answer is that he gets there with walks, not barrels. A 12.3% walk rate paired with a 16.4% strikeout rate is a genuinely rare plate discipline profile for a catcher, and a 27.0% chase rate that most hitters would envy explains how he manufactures that OBP without elite raw power. The projection's .379 OBP on a .258 average isn't optimistic, it's what the contact shape and zone command actually produce. If the 5.9% barrel rate never climbs, he stays exactly what he looks like now: a patient, contact-oriented catcher whose value is built at the top of the count, worth a full lineup spot but probably not a middle-of-the-order one.

McLean's 27.9 K% sits comfortably above league average, and the contact quality numbers, 87.3 mph average exit velocity and a 6.7% barrel rate, suggest hitters aren't squaring him up when they do make contact. The tension is the 28.0% chase rate, which is below average, meaning the strikeouts are coming mostly from swings within the zone rather than from expanding it; that works until a stretch where his command wavers and the 8.7 BB% climbs further. If the walk rate stabilizes, the 3.49 xERA and a projected 179.4 innings point toward a mid-rotation starter who earns his spot; if it doesn't, you're looking at a high-strikeout innings eater who needs a short leash.

reports.name: Joe Ryan
reports.published_report: The walk rate tells most of the story: 5.4% puts him near the top of the league, and when you pair that with a 28.8% strikeout rate, you get a pitcher who controls both ends of the count well enough to post a 3.07 xERA without needing to miss bats at an elite clip. That 43.1% hard-hit rate and 10.9% barrel rate are genuinely uncomfortable numbers, and the whole profile hinges on whether hitters keep squaring him up without it translating into damage — so far, the xwOBA of .274 says they haven't. Ryan is a mid-rotation starter who is very good at his specific version of pitching: he doesn't blow you away at 93.5 mph, he doesn't generate whiffs at a special rate, but he limits free passes and forces weak enough outcomes that the run prevention holds. If the contact quality ticks up and starts converting, the floor shrinks fast.

The xBA is elite, the xSLG is not, and that gap is the whole profile: Hoerner puts the ball in play constantly, makes almost nothing hard, and survives by finding grass at an extraordinary rate. reports.name: Logan Webb

reports.name: George Kirby

The whiff rate is ordinary at 21.6%, so he's not missing many bats inside the zone, but hitters are chasing enough out of it that the damage stays suppressed: 89.6 mph average exit velocity, a 7.2% barrel rate, an xERA of 3.86. Bradley's 27.8% K rate and 96.9 mph fastball generate genuine swing-and-miss, but hitters who make contact do real damage: 45.8% hard-hit rate and 91.6 mph average exit velocity sit at the 9th and 3rd percentiles respectively, meaning almost no starter allows harder contact. His 9.4% walk rate leaves no margin, because a pitcher who can't consistently steal called strikes has nowhere to hide when barrels pile up. If the command firms, the strikeout profile supports a mid-rotation outcome; without it, a xERA of 3.78 becomes the ceiling, propped up by strikeouts that aren't guaranteed to keep coming.

reports.name: Casey Mize
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.01 and the walk rate at 5.7%, and those two numbers together tell you what Mize actually is: a contact manager who earns his outs without needing to blow anyone away. His 93.5 mph fastball is below average, and he's not generating elite chase at 29.3%, so the 28.7% whiff rate is doing real work — hitters who make contact against him aren't doing much damage, with hard-hit rate at 34.6% and average exit velocity at 88.1 mph. If he takes the ball every fifth day and logs something close to the projected 136.8 innings, he profiles as a mid-rotation contributor with a 3.23 ERA; if the injury history reasserts itself, what's left is a very pretty partial-season line that doesn't move the needle in Detroit.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile splits cleanly in two: elite contact quality, ugly swing decisions. A 12.4% barrel rate and 90.9 mph average exit velocity put the raw power in a real place, but a 34.6% whiff rate and 34.0% chase rate explain why the xBA sits at .246 and the K% runs at 26.2%. The power translates — the projection carries him to 32 home runs across 628 plate appearances, a .474 SLG, and that's believable given the quality-of-contact shape. Everything hinges on whether pitchers keep attacking him with breaking stuff outside the zone, because if the chase rate stays where it is, that .314 OBP is about the ceiling of what the walk rate can prop up. Good everyday second baseman, full stop, with a strikeout problem baked in.

The 3.60 ERA projection is doing real work to bridge from a 4.34 xERA, and that gap lives or dies on whether he keeps the walks this suppressed while his whiff rate, a middling 23.4%, doesn't slip further. reports.name: Jacob Wilson
reports.published_report: The contact skill is genuine and the power ceiling is not. A 15.2% whiff rate ranks among the cleanest in the league, but 84.0 mph average exit velocity and a 1.6% barrel rate mean Wilson is making soft, frequent contact rather than doing damage with it — his xSLG sits at .336, and the .405 SLG in the projection reflects the gap between what he's built to do and what he'd need to do to be an above-average offensive shortstop. The walk rate at 4.8% is thin enough that the contact quality has to carry nearly everything, and if pitchers learn to work him in the zone, that 40.1% chase rate suggests they won't even need to go outside it. Elite glove (95th-percentile OAA) saves the profile: without it, this is a bench piece; with it, he's a low-end regular who wins his job with the leather and hopes the bat is just good enough not to give it back.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile flatters him more than the fastball will let him keep. A 3.22 xERA with a 28.7% strikeout rate and a 30.0% whiff rate is a genuine skill set — the chase rate at 33.9% shows hitters aren't just fouling off pitches in the zone, they're expanding. But the fastball sits at 91.7 mph, bottoming out near the seventh percentile among pitchers, and the spin behind it is equally thin at 2184 rpm, so the strikeout profile is entirely dependent on secondary stuff continuing to do the heavy lifting. If the offspeed arsenal flattens or opponents adjust, there's no heater to fall back on. The 4.15 ERA projection against a 3.22 xERA reflects exactly that gap: the underlying contact management is credible across a meaningful sample, but the walks at 8.4% are neutral and the fastball vulnerability will cost him innings in bunches, which is why the projection lands him at 114.6 innings as a swing piece rather than a rotation anchor.

reports.name: Gabriel Moreno

His 89.5 mph average exit velocity is exactly league average, yet his xwOBA sits at .362, which tells you he's earning those numbers by finding gaps and putting the ball where it needs to go, not by overwhelming anyone. The projection, .290/.369/.430 over 462 plate appearances, is a catcher hitting near the top of his lineup slot, and it holds as long as his plate discipline (10.9% walks, 15.4% strikeouts) stays intact, because if the zone judgment slips, the power isn't there to compensate. Catch that kind of contact skill behind the dish and you have a genuine above-average offensive catcher; let the discipline erode and you have a useful regular who grades out fine without standing out anywhere.

reports.name: Gregory Soto
reports.published_report: The 10.1% walk rate is the whole tension in this profile. Soto gets hitters out, a 27.8% strikeout rate, an xERA of 3.31, and average exit velocity at 85.9 mph that puts him in a different tier from most relievers, but the chase rate of 28.9% tells you why the walks keep coming: he's not pulling hitters out of the zone, he's overpowering them when they swing. That's a fragile formula for save situations, where extra baserunners compound fast. The projection splitting 17 saves and 11 holds on a 3.89 ERA feels about right: he's good enough to close, not reliable enough to own the job unchallenged.
